say: In PostgreSQL, an UPDATE does not overwrite your row.
cap: In PostgreSQL, an UPDATE does *not* *overwrite* your row.

say: It writes a brand new version, and the old one stays behind.
cap: It writes a *new* *version,* and the old one stays behind.

say: Here is one employee, Ravi, earning fifty thousand.
cap: Here is one employee, Ravi, earning 50000.

say: The hidden column C T I D shows where this row version lives. Page zero, slot one.
cap: Hidden column *ctid* = where it lives: page 0, slot *1.*

say: Now we update his salary to sixty thousand.
Same row? Look at the C T I D. It is now page zero, slot two.
cap: Same row? ctid is now page 0, slot *2.*

say: The new version went into a new slot. Stay till the end to see what happens to the old one.
cap: New version, new slot. Stay till the end for the *old* *one.*

say: This is M V C C, multiversion concurrency control.
The old version is kept while another transaction may still need to see it.
cap: The old version stays while *another* *transaction* may still see it.

say: X min changed too. In our test it went from seven fifty to seven fifty one, the transaction that wrote the new version.
cap: xmin changed too: *750* to *751,* the transaction that wrote it.

say: When no transaction needs the old version any more, it is a dead row.
cap: When nobody needs it any more, it is a *dead* *row.*

say: pg stat user tables showed one live row and one dead row.
VACUUM removes dead row versions and marks the space for reuse.
cap: *VACUUM* removes dead rows and marks the space for *reuse.*

say: After VACUUM, one live row, zero dead.
Plain VACUUM usually does not give that space back to the operating system.
cap: Plain VACUUM usually does *not* give space back to the OS.

say: So lots of updates without vacuum means a bloated table.
cap: Lots of updates without vacuum = a *bloated* *table.*
